payload.title: What Are the Armenian Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with an Armenian-Australian partner or family, who want to understand the customs their families will expect, from the formal asking to the church crowning and the lavash at the door, and to know whether marrying in Armenia itself is practical and legal.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed straight after the legal section on marrying in Armenia.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, after the legal section)
payload.angle: We follow an Armenian wedding in the order families actually live it, from the khosk-kap asking to the godparents, the church crowning and the lavash and plate at the groom's door, source each custom from UNESCO, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin and academic sources, mark what is only 'often told', and close with what page-one listicles skip: the Smartraveller level for Armenia (with the 5 km Azerbaijan border band), the fact that Australia's consular cover sits in Moscow, and the civil-registration steps Australians need for a legal wedding there, plus how Armenian-Australian couples keep these customs at home.
must_include: One framing line early: customs are kept in Armenia and across the diaspora, including Australia, and vary by family and region; differences named only where sourced
The sequence in order: asking, engagement, godparents, dressing and collection, church crowning, lavash and plate, welcome at the groom's home, music and dance
Armenian Apostolic crowning (psak) with crowns, shared cup and the kavor's role, from the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin or academic source
UNESCO lavash (2014), duduk (2008) and Kochari (2017) only in the words UNESCO's own pages support, title and year checked live

Legal section for Australians: Smartraveller overall Level 2 and Level 4 within 5 km of the Azerbaijan border (neutral wording), Australian Embassy Moscow covers Armenia, civil registration vs church wedding, CNI, apostille, translation, recognition in Australia, 'as at November 2026', 'check with the registry and the embassy, including any fees'
Armenian-Australian weddings at home: how couples keep the customs in Australia (church crowning in an Australian Armenian Apostolic parish only if sourced)

tradition_plan.note: Planner fact-checks in 2 parallel batches with separate scratch folders (02-research/batch-a, 02-research/batch-b), 15 min HARD, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds. Preferred sources: UNESCO ICH (ich.unesco.org), Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin (armenianchurch.org), Armenian Apostolic dioceses (including the Diocese of Australia and New Zealand), Armenia's Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sports (escs.am), Armenia's tourism committee (armenia.travel), History Museum of Armenia, Matenadaran, Britannica, peer-reviewed journals and the Armenian Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography. Never competitor wedding sites, Wikipedia or lifestyle magazines as sole source. Unsourced becomes 'often told' or is dropped; no [[VERIFY]] on 'often told' customs. Armenian terms transliterated as the source spells them. Smartraveller and old page already fetched (02-research/pages/); do not re-fetch.
tradition_plan.count: 11 customs plus the legal section (6 in batch A, 5 customs plus legal in batch B)

batch_B.tradition: LEGAL: marrying in Armenia as Australians
facts_to_source: whether a church wedding alone is legally valid or civil registration is required (Armenia's Family Code or Civil Status Acts Registration Agency, Ministry of Justice)

documents for foreigners: passport, CNI from Australia (DFAT or Australian Embassy Moscow page), apostille (Armenia and Australia in the Hague Apostille Convention: confirm), certified Armenian translation
recognition in Australia (Attorney-General's Department or Marriage Act 1961 s 88D); link to /expert-advice/do-you-have-to-register-an-overseas-marriage-at-home

fees: 'check with the registry and the embassy, including any fees', as at November 2026
